findings: Species identity is convincing: the primary specimen and both supplementary studies show the plain brown upperparts, dingy gray-brown throat and breast fading gradually into whitish underparts, small rounded head, short dark bill, dark eye, broad pointed wing, and short approximately square, shallowly notched tail documented by All About Birds, Audubon, and eBird.

The primary specimen is a single complete perched bird with one head, one bill, one tail, and anatomically convincing near-side wing, leg, and foot attachments; the far-side wing and leg are naturally occluded by the side-on pose. No visible eye, limb, or foot is broken or duplicated.

The detached extended-wing study is clearly supplementary and anatomically coherent, with layered coverts, secondaries, and long pointed primaries. The detached head study is likewise clearly separate; its short bill is complete and consistent with the primary head.

The illustration is somewhat rounder and fuller-bodied than the clearest perched reference photos, but it retains the species' small-headed, long-winged swallow structure and does not materially suggest another species.
The common name, scientific name “Stelgidopteryx serripennis,” and family “Hirundinidae” are correctly spelled and independently supported by the direct source pages.

Every printed measurement matches the proposed profile and the All About Birds measurements: length 12–15 cm (4.7–5.9 in), wingspan 27–30 cm (10.6–11.8 in), and weight 10–18 g (0.3–0.6 oz). Audubon independently agrees on the 12–15 cm length and 27–30 cm wingspan while publishing a narrower 11–14 g weight range; this does not invalidate the directly supported 10–18 g profile range.
The habitat paragraph is complete, grammatical, and consistent with direct descriptions of open country near water, burrow nesting in banks, and use of structural crevices or cavities.

The behavior paragraph is complete and consistent with direct accounts of low aerial foraging, relatively slow deliberate wingbeats, solitary or small-group activity, and perching on exposed branches or wires.

All six field-mark bullets are complete and correctly worded. Their claims agree with the source descriptions and attached references, including the unpatterned brown upperparts, diffuse dingy breast wash, short dark bill, relatively broad pointed wings, short square or slightly notched tail, and short dark legs and feet.
The four palette labels—WARM BROWN, GRAY-BROWN, DIRTY WHITE, and CHARCOAL BLACK—are legible and correspond appropriately to the depicted plumage and bare-part colors.

The vertical measurement diagram is internally consistent: 12 cm (4.7 in) is at the bottom, 15 cm (5.9 in) is at the top, and the values increase upward. It is explicitly labeled “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE,” while the separate “BODY LENGTH: 12–15 cm (4.7–5.9 in)” marker agrees with it.
No place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, observation locality, or other local-observation detail appears.
